A C Repair in Pasadena, TX, Where Half the Homes Predate 1977

Pasadena grew from about 3,400 people in 1940 to nearly 59,000 by 1960, and many of those houses are now on their third or fourth air conditioner. Call the free line any hour to reach an independent, locally owned HVAC company that works in Pasadena.

Most people searching for a c repair in Pasadena are living in a house that was built for a different era of cooling. Census estimates put the median year built for Pasadena homes at 1977, so half the housing is older than that. Below is what is different about keeping a Pasadena home cool, and how a free call reaches a local company.

Houston Air & Heating answers the phone; it does not fix equipment. A recorded assistant takes your call, notes whether the house is too hot or too cold and what you are seeing, and connects you with a heating and cooling business in the Pasadena area that is locally owned and runs on its own. That business sends someone out, diagnoses the problem, names its price and handles the repair. Your payment goes to that business, never to the line.

Pasadena: from strawberry fields to the Ship Channel

Pasadena was laid out in 1893 by John H. Burnett, a Galveston businessman, who borrowed the name of the California city for the green, lush look of the land. After the 1900 Galveston hurricane, the American Red Cross under Clara Barton sent 1.5 million strawberry plants to farmers in the Pasadena area, and Pasadena became the strawberry capital of the region.

The Houston Ship Channel changed everything. Refineries rose along the channel, and after World War II it became a center of the petrochemical industry. Pasadena went from 3,436 residents in 1940 to 22,483 in 1950 and 58,737 in 1960, according to the Handbook of Texas. Those plant workers needed houses fast, and a large share of the city's streets were built in those two decades.

A Pasadena house by era: what to ask the technician about

A rough guide only. Remodels and past replacements change the picture, so let the company confirm what is in your attic, closet and side yard.

Built in the 1940s to 1960s boom

Many of these homes were not designed around central air, so the air handler and ducts were fitted in later wherever they would go. Ask whether the return air opening is big enough for the system and whether long duct runs to the back bedrooms leak.

Built in the 1970s and 1980s

Central air from the start, but the original equipment is long gone and the ducts may be the same age as the roof. Ask whether a replacement is being sized to the house, with a load calculation, rather than copied from the old unit's label.

East of 146, in the windstorm area

For homes in Pasadena's windstorm area, new work and repairs are expected to meet TDI's windstorm building standards. Ask whether the outdoor unit will be anchored to its pad and whether the job will be inspected for a windstorm certificate.

The windstorm rule that applies to only part of Pasadena

Pasadena is unusual among Harris County suburbs. The Texas Department of Insurance treats the part of the city that lies east of State Highway 146, inside the city limits, as a designated catastrophe area, the same status as the first tier counties on the coast. TDI added that part of Pasadena by a commissioner's order after a November 1996 hearing, along with nearby Shoreacres, at the request of both cities.

Why does that matter for air conditioning? To qualify for wind and hail coverage through the Texas Windstorm Insurance Association, new work and repairs in a catastrophe area must meet TDI building specifications and pass inspection, and TDI issues a separate windstorm certificate for the air conditioner once it is installed and inspected. In practice the focus is on the outdoor condenser: TDI's product evaluation rules for condenser anchorage call for a pad large and thick enough to take the fasteners and an anchoring method that keeps the unit from overturning. A loose condenser can shift in a hurricane, kink its refrigerant lines or turn into flying debris.

If your house is on the bay side of 146, raise this before you sign for a new system. Ask the company whether the unit will be anchored to the windstorm standard, who arranges the TDI or engineer inspection, and whether you will get the certificate for your records. If you live west of 146, which covers most of Pasadena, the windstorm program does not apply to you.

City permits for AC work in Pasadena

Pasadena runs its own Permit Department, which handles building and mechanical permits inside the city limits and publishes a fee schedule. The city also requires paperwork showing compliance with the state's energy code before it signs off on covered work. For a homeowner the takeaway is short: ask whether your system change needs a city permit and inspection, and make sure the quote you sign names both if it does.

Quick checks before you call

  • Thermostat. Set to Cool, a few degrees below room temperature, with fresh batteries if it uses them.
  • Air filter. Lint and dust can smother a filter until the indoor coil ices over. Put in a clean one if yours looks matted.
  • Breaker. Flip the AC breaker back on once if it has tripped. Should it pop again, something is wrong, so stop there and phone for help.
  • Outdoor unit. Pull back grass clippings, leaves and anything stacked against the condenser so it can move air.

Anything past that, including refrigerant, wiring and the parts inside the panels, is a job for a technician. Our guide to an AC that is not cooling walks through the common causes.

Verify the license before work begins. Texas requires anyone contracting to do air conditioning, refrigeration or heating work to hold an Air Conditioning and Refrigeration (ACR) Contractor license from the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR). Ask the company for its ACR license number, then confirm it on the TDLR license search (opens in a new tab). The line does not check this for you.

Common questions

Who do I call for a c repair in Pasadena, TX at night?

Call the free line. A recorded assistant picks up day or night, takes a quick description of the trouble, and puts you through to a Pasadena-area HVAC business that is locally owned and independent of the line. If the company cannot pick up right then, your name, number and problem are passed on so it can call you back. The company quotes and bills you directly.

Does my AC need a windstorm inspection in Pasadena?

Only if the home is in the part of Pasadena that the Texas Department of Insurance (TDI) treats as a catastrophe area: east of State Highway 146 and inside the city limits. There, work on a home that carries or wants wind coverage through the Texas Windstorm Insurance Association is inspected, and TDI lists air conditioner units among the items it certifies. West of 146, which is most of the city, this rule does not apply.

Does Pasadena require a permit for a new air conditioner?

Expect one inside city limits. Pasadena has its own Permit Department, and its published fee schedule covers mechanical work. Requirements can differ by job, so before you agree to a price, ask the company whether your replacement needs a city permit, who will apply for it, and make sure the quote shows it.

Who is the electric company in Pasadena, Texas?

CenterPoint Energy owns the poles and wires in Pasadena and handles outages, and because Pasadena is in the competitive retail market you buy power from a retail provider you choose. Neither one repairs air conditioners. Lights on and a silent AC means the fault is in the cooling system, which is HVAC company work.

Is it worth fixing an old AC in a 1960s Pasadena house?

It depends on what failed. A fan motor or a capacitor can be a reasonable repair even on an older unit. A failed compressor or a leaking coil on an old system pushes the numbers toward replacement. In an older house, also ask whether the ducts and return air were checked, because a new unit hooked to tired ducts can still cool poorly.
